title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning
authors: Sepehr Mousavi, Levi Lingsch, Siddhartha Mishra, Laura De Lorenzis
abstract: Neural operators fit their representation of functions to the task they are trained on, so every new task rebuilds a reduced space from labeled data. Following the self-supervised pre-training that made representations shareable in natural language processing and computer vision, we decouple representation learning from operator learning. A functional autoencoder is pre-trained on analytic functions synthesized on the fly, with no solver and no labels, to represent functions on arbitrary point clouds, and the latent space it induces is frozen and reused across tasks. The representation is exactly equivariant to translation, dilation, and amplitude, and reconstructs solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) and natural images on geometries it never saw. Being task-agnostic, the latent space can be interpreted in its own right. The whole space is used and decodes to valid fields, it preserves the ordering of distances between physical fields, its geodesics interpolate physical evolutions, and edit directions transfer across fields. With frozen representation maps, a dataset is encoded once and a neural operator is trained entirely on cached embeddings, which saves memory and training time. On 28 tasks in fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, acoustics, and the Helmholtz and Poisson equations, this paradigm can exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end architectures, with up to an order of magnitude higher throughput and memory savings that fit models nearly two orders of magnitude larger on consumer-grade GPUs. At inference, latent rollouts run up to an order of magnitude faster than regular rollouts, and chunked inference processes functions of over half a billion points on a single consumer-grade GPU.

infographic.key_insight: A self-supervised functional autoencoder learns a reusable latent space, separating function representation from task-specific operator learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For solid-mechanics surrogates, frozen representations can reduce training memory and time while supporting fields sampled on arbitrary point clouds.
method: Pre-train on analytically generated functions without solvers or labels.
Freeze translation-, dilation-, and amplitude-equivariant representation maps and cache dataset embeddings.
Train task-specific neural operators in latent space and decode predicted fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 28 tasks spanning solid mechanics and other PDE domains, the abstract reports accuracy that can exceed state-of-the-art end-to-end models, up to 10× higher throughput, and chunked inference on over half a billion points.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy and efficiency gains should be verified for the target mechanics regime; the abstract does not establish performance for every material law or boundary condition.
infographic.paper_title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning

title: A Tensor-Network Chebyshev--Galerkin Method for Boundary-Value Problems in Computational Mechanics
authors: Juan José Rodríguez-Aldavero, Ángel de la Rosa Velasco, Juan José García-Ripoll
abstract: Quantum-inspired numerical methods for partial differential equations represent discretized fields and operators as quantics tensor trains (QTT), so that their cost depends on how compressible the problem is rather than on the number of unknowns. Global spectral formulations in this setting have so far relied on Fourier bases, restricted to periodic problems, or on collocation, which does not preserve the variational structure exploited by tensor-network solvers. We introduce a QTT Chebyshev--Galerkin method that assembles and solves global spectral systems directly in compressed form, without forming the underlying arrays. Starting from the weak formulation, the method handles coupled elliptic systems with variable coefficients, smoothly mapped geometries, and mixed Dirichlet--Robin boundary conditions, and yields symmetric positive-definite systems suited to variational tensor-network solvers. Parameters and random inputs enter as additional coordinates, so the same construction returns the solution over an entire parameter space in a single solve. In linear elasticity, the method retains spectral convergence and reaches errors below $10^{-8}$ on a three-dimensional benchmark, beyond those attained by QTT finite differences and Q2/Q4 FEniCSx finite elements over the tested range. A six-parameter cantilever design study covering $1.7\times10^{7}$ designs is solved in a single 92~s run, and a stochastic problem with ten random coordinates is represented with $2.4\times10^{6}$ times less memory than its full coefficient array.

infographic.key_insight: A quantics tensor-train (QTT) Chebyshev–Galerkin method solves global spectral boundary-value problems directly in compressed form while preserving their variational structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method enables accurate linear-elasticity analysis across large design and uncertainty spaces without explicitly storing full solution arrays.
method: Assemble weak-form spectral systems directly as QTT representations.
Handle variable coefficients, mapped geometries, and mixed Dirichlet–Robin conditions.
Treat parameters and random inputs as extra coordinates for a single joint solve.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports errors below 10⁻⁸ on a 3D elasticity benchmark, 1.7×10⁷ cantilever designs solved in 92 s, and 2.4×10⁶-fold memory reduction versus a full coefficient array for a ten-random-coordinate problem.
infographic.watch_item: Computational savings depend on tensor compressibility; the reported benchmarks do not establish comparable gains for poorly compressible problems.
infographic.paper_title: A Tensor-Network Chebyshev--Galerkin Method for Boundary-Value Problems in Computational Mechanics

title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
authors: Li Zheng, Simin Chen
abstract: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.

infographic.key_insight: CloakFEM shows that valid, solvable FEM programs can act as efficiency attacks, dramatically increasing solver work without causing execution failure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation services may need resource-aware safeguards because successful FEM execution does not guarantee computationally safe workloads.
method: Use an LLM agent to search for computationally expensive FEM programs.
Guide generation with an FEM-specific intermediate representation.
Apply a deterministic validity gate to enforce runnable constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM outperformed five generic black-box baselines; the largest reported iteration increase was 43 to 247,367 (5,752.72×).
infographic.watch_item: Iteration amplification is not necessarily proportional to wall-clock slowdown, and vulnerability may depend on the solver and problem configuration.
infographic.paper_title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion

title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks
authors: Manish Kumar Singh, Dominic Kang Jueh Lim, Anson Wen Han Cheong, Adams Wai Kin Kong, Chang Quan Lai
abstract: Current methods of deriving ultrastiff isotropic metamaterials require heuristics or topology optimization, which are highly inefficient and limited by human input. To circumvent this, Physics Informed Neural Networks are applied to analytical equations to systematically solve for plate orientations in closed cell lattices. Following a standardized procedure, the plate orientations were modelled and assembled into geometries resembling quasi random foams for validation via finite element simulations. Closed cell 6-plate geometries were also additively manufactured using LAPIS and experimentally characterized. The results indicate that a minimum of 6 plates is required to constitute an ultrastiff isotropic lattice, 7 plates would return the established plate Cubic Octet structure while 8 to 10 plate geometries did not show significant differences in properties. Despite the introduction of some plate bending due to sub-optimal plate placement strategy, relative stiffness of the PINNs lattices adheres closely to the Hashin Shtrikman upper bound, 90 percent of Hashin Shtrikman upper bound at a relative density of 0.4, and the lattices maintain near isotropic behaviour, achieving a Zener ratio of 0.95 at a relative density of 0.1. Benchmarking results show that specific stiffness of PINNs lattices is higher than the majority of isotropic architectures reported in the literature.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed neural networks identify plate orientations for near-isotropic, ultrastiff lattices, with six plates found to be the minimum required.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These architectures offer a systematic route to lightweight structures with high specific stiffness and nearly direction-independent elastic response.
method: Apply PINNs to analytical equations to solve for plate orientations.
Assemble orientations into closed-cell, quasi-random foam geometries and evaluate them using finite element simulations.
Additively manufacture six-plate geometries using LAPIS and characterize them experimentally.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported lattices reach 90% of the Hashin–Shtrikman stiffness upper bound at relative density 0.4 and a near-isotropic Zener ratio of 0.95 at relative density 0.1.
infographic.watch_item: Suboptimal plate placement introduces bending, so orientation solutions alone do not guarantee realization of the theoretical stiffness limit.
infographic.paper_title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks

title: Geometric Multigrid Preconditioners for conforming Finite Element Methods on Arbitrarily Agglomerated Meshes
authors: Santiago Badia, Jordi Manyer
abstract: Geometric multigrid methods for conforming finite element discretisations classically require a nested mesh hierarchy, forcing coarse meshes to be conforming, which is unsuitable for general domains. In order to eliminate this geometric constraint, we introduce and analyse a family of multilevel auxiliary space preconditioners. At the first level, a conforming Lagrangian discretisation on a fine simplicial mesh is preconditioned by a non-conforming polytopal discretisation posed on an arbitrarily agglomerated coarse mesh. At the subsequent levels, the coarse problem is solved by a geometric multigrid method for that polytopal discretisation on further agglomerated meshes, so that the whole hierarchy is generated from the fine mesh by agglomeration alone. We consider two polytopal discretisations, a symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method and a hybrid high-order method. The prolongation operator at the first level is an element-wise interpolation onto the fine mesh followed by nodal averaging, preceded in the hybrid high-order case by a local potential reconstruction. For point-Jacobi and vertex-star patch additive Schwarz smoothers, we prove that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by $O((H/h)^3)$, where $H/h$ is the coarsening ratio, and by $O((H/h)^2)$ for the DG variant with penalty proportional to $H/h$. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions, on structured and unstructured meshes with agglomerates generated by automatic clustering algorithms, confirm the robustness of the preconditioners.

infographic.key_insight: Auxiliary-space multigrid preconditioners remove the need for nested conforming coarse meshes by building the hierarchy through arbitrary mesh agglomeration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers robust preconditioning for conforming finite element systems on general domains where constructing conforming coarse meshes is difficult.
method: Couple fine-mesh conforming Lagrange elements to coarse polytopal DG or hybrid high-order discretisations.
Transfer coarse solutions by element-wise interpolation and nodal averaging, with local potential reconstruction for the hybrid high-order variant.
Apply multigrid on further agglomerated meshes using point-Jacobi or vertex-star additive Schwarz smoothing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Condition-number bounds scale as O((H/h)^3), improving to O((H/h)^2) for DG with appropriately scaled penalties; 2D and 3D tests on structured and unstructured meshes confirm robustness.
infographic.watch_item: The bounds worsen with the coarsening ratio H/h, so aggressive agglomeration may reduce preconditioner effectiveness.
infographic.paper_title: Geometric Multigrid Preconditioners for conforming Finite Element Methods on Arbitrarily Agglomerated Meshes

title: Remap for ALE Hydrodynamics via Direct Interpolation and Constraint Optimization
authors: Brendan Keith, Dohyun Kim, Boyan Lazarov, Ketan Mittal, Cosmin G. Petra, Mathias R. Schmidt
abstract: This work presents an optimization-based remap approach for arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) hydrodynamics that preserves sharp features and physical bounds while conserving global quantities such as volume, mass, momentum, and total energy. Achieving these properties is the main challenge in remap methods. The presented approach is well-suited for high-order finite element (FE) discretizations and ALE methods that allow for large, purely Lagrangian displacements between successive remeshing and remapping steps. Recent advances in parallel, GPU-capable interpolation routines enable the initial transfer of all fields via direct physical-space interpolation, avoiding computationally costly and diffusive pseudo-transient PDE-based advection. The interpolation produces bounded fields with minimal numerical diffusion. However, it may violate the desired conservation of global properties. Thus, a subsequent optimization step restores conservation while preserving physical bounds. The presented method provides minimally diffusive remapping of finite element fields of arbitrary order. Moreover, it directly remaps quantities defined at integration points, eliminating the need for projection onto finite element spaces. The approach also mitigates typical challenges associated with synchronizing primal variables and conserved quantities in advection-based remap methods. The proposed optimization-based remap method is evaluated using standard two- and three-dimensional remap benchmarks and full ALE hydrodynamics simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Direct interpolation followed by constraint optimization enables minimally diffusive ALE remapping while enforcing global conservation and physical bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports high-order hydrodynamics simulations with large Lagrangian mesh displacements while preserving sharp features and conserving volume, mass, momentum, and total energy.
method: Transfer fields by direct physical-space interpolation using parallel, GPU-capable routines.
Restore global conservation through optimization while preserving physical bounds.
Remap arbitrary-order finite element fields and integration-point quantities without intermediate projection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is evaluated on standard 2D and 3D remap benchmarks and full ALE hydrodynamics simulations; the abstract reports no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The computational cost and parallel scalability of the conservation-restoring optimization require assessment for large simulations.
infographic.paper_title: Remap for ALE Hydrodynamics via Direct Interpolation and Constraint Optimization

title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
authors: Suhas Suresh Bharadwaj
abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

infographic.key_insight: Exact boundary and initial constraints enable PINNs to identify the shear piezoelectric coefficient e15 accurately from sparse, noisy simulated wavefields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support nondestructive characterization of shear electromechanical coupling in PMUTs and SAW devices without dedicated destructive resonance tests.
method: Embed spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers into network outputs to enforce boundary and initial conditions exactly.
Train against coupled electro-elastodynamic equations and sparse observations, eliminating boundary and initial-condition penalty weights.
Nondimensionalize governing coefficients to comparable scales for optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six formulations on manufactured data at 30 dB, constrained PINNs achieved 0.15–0.51% mean e15 error; the full formulation achieved 1.19% on finite-element data sampled along one subsurface line.
infographic.watch_item: Validation uses simulated plane-strain data; robustness to experimental noise, model mismatch, and real device geometries remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 3D
authors: Tommaso Bevilacqua, Axel Klawonn, Martin Lanser, Adam Wasiak
abstract: Overlapping Schwarz methods are among the most successful domain decomposition preconditioners for large-scale finite element simulations. In this work, the Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW), GDSW$^*$, and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces are studied for three-dimensional high-order finite element method (FEM) and virtual element method (VEM) for the Poisson equation and the equations of linear elasticity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of GDSW-type coarse spaces for polynomial degrees $k\ge 3$ in three dimensions, for either discretization. In 3D VEM, the face degrees of freedom (DOFs) are moments instead of point values. The kernel of the differential operator, which defines the interface values of the GDSW coarse basis functions, must be represented through these moments. The construction is therefore no longer purely algebraic and, without this correction, the coarse level loses its effect for $k\ge 3$. FEM and VEM are tested on hexahedral meshes, and VEM is additionally tested on polyhedral ones. Polynomial degrees up to $k=5$ and runs on up to $4\,096$ subdomains and parallel cores are included in the numerical study. Numerical experiments show scalable iteration counts for all coarse space variants for the Poisson problem, illustrating the expected trade-off between the coarse space size and robustness. Further experiments for linear elasticity confirms that the moment-based construction extends naturally from the scalar to the vector-valued problem.

infographic.key_insight: GDSW-type coarse spaces enable scalable high-order 3D Schwarz preconditioning, but VEM requires moment-correct representations of the operator kernel to retain coarse-level effectiveness for k ≥ 3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These preconditioners support parallel finite element and virtual element simulations of Poisson and linear elasticity problems.
method: Study two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW, GDSW*, and reduced GDSW coarse spaces.
Represent operator-kernel interface values through face moments for high-order 3D VEM.
Evaluate FEM on hexahedral meshes and VEM on hexahedral and polyhedral meshes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests reach polynomial degree k = 5 and 4,096 subdomains and parallel cores, showing scalable Poisson iteration counts across all coarse-space variants and extension of the moment-based construction to linear elasticity.
infographic.watch_item: The VEM coarse-space construction is not purely algebraic: omitting the face-moment correction makes the coarse level ineffective for k ≥ 3.
infographic.paper_title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 3D

title: Optimal stability estimates and preasymptotic error analysis of the CIP-FEM for the Helmholtz equation with uniaxial perfectly matched layers
authors: Silin Wen, Yu Du
abstract: We study the uniaxial perfectly matched layer (UPML) problem for the Helmholtz equation in two and three dimensions and establish wavenumber-explicit stability estimates at high wavenumbers. For the full-space UPML problem, we prove the optimal stability estimate with the inf-sup constant satisfying $μ_\infty\eqsim k^{-1}$ for sufficiently large $k$ if the absorption function $σ\in W^{1,\infty}$ is a piecewise-power function of order at least one for which $\|σ'\|_{L^\infty(\{t:0<σ(t)\leqδ_*\})}\leq \varepsilon_*$, where $\varepsilon_*$ and $δ_*$ depend only on the PML parameters. Using this stability estimate, we obtain the optimal inf-sup estimate $μ_L\eqsim k^{-1}$ for the truncated UPML problem. These estimates further yield preasymptotic error estimates for a linear continuous interior penalty finite element method (CIP-FEM). Numerical simulations confirmed the theoretical predictions and demonstrated the effectiveness of CIP-FEM under high-wavenumber conditions.

infographic.key_insight: For high-wavenumber Helmholtz equations in 2D and 3D, the paper proves optimal inf-sup scaling μ ≍ k⁻¹ for full-space and truncated uniaxial perfectly matched layers, enabling preasymptotic CIP-FEM error estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results strengthen the theoretical basis for finite-element simulation of high-frequency waves with absorbing layers that represent unbounded domains.
method: Establish wavenumber-explicit stability for full-space UPML.
Transfer optimal inf-sup estimates to truncated UPML.
Derive preasymptotic error estimates for linear continuous interior penalty FEM.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations confirm the theoretical predictions and demonstrate CIP-FEM effectiveness at high wavenumbers; the abstract provides no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The stability guarantees require sufficiently large wavenumbers and specified absorption-profile regularity and small-derivative conditions near the onset of absorption.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal stability estimates and preasymptotic error analysis of the CIP-FEM for the Helmholtz equation with uniaxial perfectly matched layers

title: Process-zone condensation: a discretization-exact reduced cell model for FE$^2$ analysis of composites with fibre-matrix debonding and matrix plasticity
authors: Leonilson Toffoli Pedrini, Maycoln Conci, Rafael Marin Ferro
abstract: Periodic composites with cohesive interfaces and matrix plasticity require nonlinear cell solutions in multiscale analysis. Process-zone condensation eliminates the linear elastic remainder of the cell by a Schur complement, retaining all interfacial and process-zone internal variables. Influence matrices recover macroscopic stress and consistent tangent. One back-substitution per increment checks that the matrix outside the retained zone remains elastic. While this holds, the reduction is exact relative to the full discretisation, also with a plastic matrix, and requires no training. In an E-glass/epoxy cell, eight of nine two-dimensional paths agree with the full cell to 1e-11 in stress and tangent; the check flags the ninth. Three paths on each of two three-dimensional meshes need zone expansion. Excluding setup and checks, two-dimensional path timings show an aggregate speed-up of 3.3; certified three-dimensional zones show none. In adaptive finite element squared (FE$^2$) simulations of a perforated plate, the reduced solver reproduces the full-cell response within solver tolerances, 1.51 times faster for glass/polypropylene and slower for glass/epoxy. Independent Ansys models agree to below 1e-3 in cell stress and about 0.6% in plate reactions, although local damage and plasticity onsets differ. The advantage depends on zone size, active set and adaptation costs.

infographic.key_insight: Process-zone condensation reduces nonlinear composite-cell solves without training while remaining exact relative to the full discretization as long as the eliminated region stays elastic.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method can accelerate FE² simulations of composites with fibre–matrix debonding and matrix plasticity while preserving macroscopic stress and consistent tangent accuracy.
method: Schur-condense the linear elastic remainder, retaining all interface and process-zone internal variables.
Recover macroscopic stress and consistent tangent using influence matrices.
Back-substitute once per increment to check elasticity outside the retained zone and expand it when needed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Eight of nine 2D paths matched full-cell stress and tangent to 1e-11, with the ninth flagged; aggregate 2D path speed-up was 3.3× excluding setup and checks, while adaptive plate FE² achieved 1.51× for glass/polypropylene.
infographic.watch_item: Speed-up is not guaranteed: certified 3D zones showed none, glass/epoxy plate simulations were slower, and efficiency depends on zone size, active sets and adaptation costs.
infographic.paper_title: Process-zone condensation: a discretization-exact reduced cell model for FE$^2$ analysis of composites with fibre-matrix debonding and matrix plasticity

title: A Finite Element Model for Fluid--Poroelastic Structure Interaction with Dissipative Interface
authors: Mohammad Jannesari, Francesco Costanzo
abstract: This paper extends our prior work on interface conditions between two poroelastic domains to the case when a poroelastic domain interacts with a pure fluid. The porous medium is assumed to be deformable and modeled following mixture theory. When not in a mixture, each constituent of the porous domain is assumed to be incompressible. An arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian formulation is developed for both the fluid and porous domains. The fluid velocity and pressure fields are allowed to be discontinuous across the pure fluid/porous domain interface. A globally continuous displacement field is defined to represent both the deformation of the solid skeleton of the poroelastic medium and the mesh motion in the pure fluid domain. As an interface condition, the continuity of the normal component of the filtration velocity is enforced via a Lagrange multiplier. The mixture momentum jump condition is implemented so as to transfer the traction from the fluid side to the porous domain. A dissipative behavior is attributed to the interface, and the jump condition for the fluid momentum, derived from Hamilton's principle, incorporates this prescribed behavior. The model implementation is verified using the method of manufactured solutions, and a sample problem is solved to compare an inert interface with a fully dissipative one. The results show satisfactory convergence rates, while the proposed model successfully reproduces the analytical solution of a benchmark problem using conventional jump conditions. Furthermore, the findings highlight the significant influence of the selected interface model on the behavior of the system.

infographic.key_insight: A finite element model couples a pure fluid to a deformable poroelastic medium while allowing velocity and pressure jumps and dissipation at their interface.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Interface modeling significantly affects predicted fluid–porous structure behavior, making it important for reliable coupled-flow and deformation simulations.
method: Use mixture theory and an arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian formulation in both domains.
Represent skeleton deformation and fluid mesh motion with a globally continuous displacement field.
Enforce normal filtration continuity with a Lagrange multiplier and momentum jump conditions that account for traction transfer and interface dissipation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured-solution tests show satisfactory convergence, an analytical benchmark is reproduced, and a sample problem compares inert and fully dissipative interfaces.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports numerical verification rather than experimental validation; the interface dissipation model requires careful selection for each application.
infographic.paper_title: A Finite Element Model for Fluid--Poroelastic Structure Interaction with Dissipative Interface

title: OUCH: Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic Stimulation for Automated Neurological Assessment
authors: Sherry Choi, Sitao Sunny Li, Joseph Romero, Lillian Chin, Ashwin G. Ramayya, Allison M. Okamura
abstract: Motor responses evoked by noxious stimulation are used to assess neurological function in hospitalized patients with disorders of consciousness. In standard bedside assessments, these stimuli are applied manually, resulting in substantial variation in force, duration, frequency, and location. Here, we present OUCH (Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic stimulation), a wrist-worn device that uses pneumatic actuation to deliver noxious mechanical stimuli. OUCH combines stacked pneumatic pouch actuators, a rigid indenter, and a compliant spacer designed to buckle at a set load, so that the indenter contacts the skin only during actuation. We characterize the device using blocked force tests, clinician evaluation, finite element analysis, and a deformable pressure testbed, and benchmark it against a commercially available handheld pressure algometer. At 200 kPa pouch inflation pressure, our indenter concentrated its load into an estimated contact pressure of 18,500 kPa, over 25 times that of the algometer tip, while requiring less total force. On the deformable testbed, it localized deformation near the surface, while deformation at depth remained comparable to the algometer. As a result, in preliminary perceptual testing, our indenter elicited discomfort at approximately 89% lower applied force than the algometer, demonstrating the feasibility of evoking discomfort with a compact, wearable soft actuator. These results show that combining pneumatic actuation with designed contact geometry enables controlled, repeatable noxious stimulation at the wrist, providing a foundation for objective neurological assessment.

infographic.key_insight: OUCH combines pneumatic actuation with focused indenter geometry to deliver controlled wrist stimulation and elicit discomfort at approximately 89% lower applied force than a handheld pressure algometer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A compact wearable actuator could standardize stimulus delivery for neurological assessment while reducing reliance on variable manual techniques.
method: Stacked pneumatic pouch actuators drive a rigid indenter.
A compliant spacer buckles at a set load, allowing skin contact only during actuation.
Finite element analysis and deformable-testbed measurements characterize tissue loading.
infographic.evidence_signal: Blocked-force tests, clinician evaluation, finite element analysis, and preliminary perceptual testing supported an estimated contact pressure of 18,500 kPa at 200 kPa inflation and comparable deformation at depth to the algometer.
infographic.watch_item: Preliminary discomfort results do not establish safety or diagnostic validity in patients with disorders of consciousness.
infographic.paper_title: OUCH: Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic Stimulation for Automated Neurological Assessment

title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
authors: Zhuoli Ouyang, Changxi Chi, Siyuan Li, Tailin Wu
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, and recent methods incorporate curvature-aware strategies. However, in the high-dimensional parameter space of LLMs, these methods inherently suffer from exploding gradient variance and prohibitive costs. Conversely, confining updates to a low-dimensional subspace reduces variance but discards critical high-dimensional information, degrading performance. This creates a fundamental dilemma: full-space optimization is informative but has high variance, while subspace optimization has low variance but loses information. To break this trade-off, we propose ENGINE (Endogenous Variational MultiScale). Inspired by computational mechanics, we adapt static Variational MultiScale (VMS) theory to dynamic optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales. Through a multigrid-style V-cycle, ENGINE alternates between spaces, dynamically probing fine-grained information in the high-dimensional space and injecting it to correct the efficient low-dimensional sampling process. Under appropriate assumptions, statistical analysis characterizes variance reduction and correction of curvature-induced bias, and convergence analysis establishes a stationarity bound for the corrected coarse updates. Evaluations on standard LLM benchmarks show that ENGINE achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing ZO methods, achieving up to a $2.61\times$ speed-up in forward passes with zero additional peak memory overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/ENGINE.

infographic.key_insight: ENGINE couples low-variance subspace updates with high-dimensional corrections to improve zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning without additional peak memory overhead.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It transfers variational multiscale ideas from computational mechanics to memory-efficient optimization of large language models.
method: Treat low-dimensional and full parameter spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales.
Alternate between scales using a multigrid-style V-cycle.
Probe fine-scale information to correct coarse-space sampling and updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: On standard LLM benchmarks, the abstract reports higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing zeroth-order methods, with up to 2.61× speed-up measured in forward passes and zero additional peak memory overhead.
infographic.watch_item: Theoretical guarantees depend on assumptions, and forward-pass savings do not necessarily translate directly into wall-clock speed-ups.
infographic.paper_title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning

title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning
authors: Tom Saliencro, Wen-Hsuan Liu, Rohan Desai, Amara Okonkwo, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

infographic.key_insight: BISECT improves continual learning by splitting low-rank updates into shared and novel feature directions rather than treating all cross-task overlap as interference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support sequential adaptation of vision-based engineering inspection models, though solid-mechanics applications are not evaluated in the abstract.
method: Partition a fixed LoRA rank budget into dominant joint historical–current modes and an orthogonal novelty complement.
Extract novelty directions using generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection.
Merge trained updates into the frozen backbone, gating shared rank-1 atoms by current-to-joint Rayleigh ratios and preserving novelty atoms at unit gain.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight incremental settings on five vision datasets, BISECT reportedly outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines without extra inference parameters or FLOPs; historical null tails capture only 5.5% of incoming-task variance.
infographic.watch_item: Training-time costs and numerical stability of Gram-matrix decomposition and whitening are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning

title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA
authors: Wen-Hsuan Liu, Amara Okonkwo, Tom Saliencro, Rohan Desai, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers largely relies on a costly premise: preventing catastrophic forgetting requires either spawning a dedicated LoRA branch per session---causing adapter parameters to scale linearly with task horizon---or applying sparse Mixture-of-Experts gating symmetrically to both forward and backward passes, which sacrifices representational rank at test time. We argue that reading consolidated knowledge and writing new task credit are fundamentally asymmetric operations. Because visual features in a shared low-rank space distribute across rank-1 atoms rather than localizing in disjoint task silos, forward inference should read all atoms at full rank capacity, whereas backward optimization should restrict plasticity to a sparse subset of input-aligned channels. We introduce RASP (Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity LoRA), which adapts a single stationary-size adapter across sequential tasks. At each step, a scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-$q$ unlocked atoms to receive gradients, blocks updates on the remaining $r-q$ channels, and penalizes Frobenius Gram coherence between active and non-updated output directions. Across sessions, the router's empirical activation trace and each atom's exact spectral norm form a zero-overhead geometric consolidation index $ω_j = \sqrt{\tilde{c}_j \tildeσ_j}$ that drives Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking. Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA learners under a strictly constant parameter footprint.

infographic.key_insight: RASP separates reading from learning: inference uses all LoRA atoms, while updates target only a sparse subset within a fixed-size adapter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support memory-bounded continual adaptation of engineering vision systems, but the abstract does not evaluate constitutive modeling or solid mechanics tasks.
method: A scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-q unlocked atoms for gradient updates while preserving full-rank adapter access during inference.
A Gram-coherence penalty discourages overlap between active and non-updated output directions.
Activation history and atom spectral norms guide Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking to protect consolidated knowledge.
infographic.evidence_signal: On CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, the abstract reports matching or exceeding branch-expanding LoRA learners with constant adapter parameter count, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Atom locking may constrain future learning over long task sequences; constant parameter count alone does not establish sustained adaptability.
infographic.paper_title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA

title: Optimal Error Estimates With Polynomial Dependence on $ε^{-1}$ for Mixed Finite Element Methods of the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes System
authors: Haijun Gao, Xi Li, Xiaoli Li
abstract: In this paper, we analyze a first-order convex-splitting mixed finite element scheme for the Cahn--Hilliard--Navier--Stokes system, tracking explicitly how the error constants depend on the interface width $ε$. Due to the strong nonlinear coupling inherent in the CHNS system and the singular dependence of the Cahn--Hilliard equation on $ε$, conventional energy-based analyzes often lead to severe dependence of the error constants on $ε^{-1}$, and may even result in exponential growth. Such dependence significantly limits the applicability of the resulting error estimates in the small-interfacial-thickness regime. To overcome this difficulty, we develop a robust parameter error analysis framework with respect to interfacial thickness $ε$. In particular, by introducing $H^{-1}$ approximation properties for the Ritz projection and the Ritz and Stokes quasi-projection operators, together with spectral-type estimates for the discrete perturbed Cahn--Hilliard operator, we effectively control the singular terms arising from the interfacial thickness parameter in the error analysis. Compared with the classical results, which address only the Allen-Cahn or Cahn-Hilliard equation, we adopt a three-term discrete Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality analysis technique and achieve a substantial reduction in the degree of polynomial dependence for the coupled system. Numerical experiments are presented to verify the effectiveness of the theoretical results and to demonstrate the robustness of the method for different parameters of interfacial thickness.

infographic.key_insight: The analysis establishes optimal error estimates with polynomial, rather than potentially exponential, dependence on inverse interface width for a mixed finite element scheme of the coupled Cahn–Hilliard–Navier–Stokes system.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These estimates strengthen confidence in finite element simulations of two-phase flows with thin diffuse interfaces.
method: Analyze a first-order convex-splitting mixed finite element scheme.
Combine H⁻¹ approximation properties of Ritz and Stokes projections with discrete Cahn–Hilliard spectral estimates.
Use a three-term discrete Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality to reduce the degree of polynomial parameter dependence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments test the theoretical results and demonstrate robustness across different interface-width parameters; the abstract provides no quantitative errors or convergence rates.
infographic.watch_item: Polynomial dependence still allows error constants to grow as interface width decreases; the abstract does not specify mesh or time-step restrictions.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal Error Estimates With Polynomial Dependence on $ε^{-1}$ for Mixed Finite Element Methods of the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes System

title: Manifold Embedding of Deep Image Features for Image Matching via Neural Adjoint Maps
authors: Nafie El Amrani, Moritz Heep, Florian Bernard
abstract: Estimating semantic correspondences between different object instances of similar categories in real-world images is a fundamental challenge in computer vision. While the recent progress in foundation models has significantly advanced solutions for such difficult image correspondence problems, respective methods are often insufficiently regularised. For example, common nearest-neighbour matching with foundation model features often results in noisy correspondences, which is particularly prominent when solving for dense correspondences. In this work, we tackle image matching via functional maps, which have been popularised for 3D shape matching due to their powerful spectral formalism utilising an efficient low-dimensional linear representation. However, functional maps require that domains (in our cases the rectangular image grids) are equipped with an informative and non-trivial geometry. To define a meaningful manifold structure for images, we use Galerkin's method from finite elements to derive a discrete Laplace-Beltrami operator (LBO) based on a manifold embedding of deep image features. Further, we leverage a neural adjoint map that allows to represent non-linear mappings. We demonstrate that our method sets the new state of the art among zero-shot image correspondence methods on multiple dense correspondence benchmarks of real-world images. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/NafieAmrani/NAMI

infographic.key_insight: Embedding deep image features into a manifold enables geometry-aware semantic image matching with spectral regularisation and non-linear neural adjoint maps.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work transfers finite-element and spectral geometry tools to image correspondence, rather than developing a solid-mechanics or FEM surrogate model.
method: Construct a meaningful image manifold from deep feature embeddings.
Use finite-element Galerkin discretisation to derive a Laplace–Beltrami operator for spectral functional maps.
Leverage a neural adjoint map to represent non-linear correspondences.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on multiple real-world dense image correspondence benchmarks, without naming datasets or providing numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Matching quality may depend on the geometry induced by the deep features; robustness to domain shifts is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Manifold Embedding of Deep Image Features for Image Matching via Neural Adjoint Maps

title: Coupled Soft-Clamped Polygon Resonators with Tunable Mechanical Coupling
authors: Zhihao Niu, Peng Chen, Shenggen Zheng, Yuan-Yuan Zhao, Yuanyuan Zhao
abstract: Coupler geometry controls both the frequency splitting and the dissipation of coupled polygon resonators. We develop a continuum model for two identical square-shaped resonators coupled by a shared tether and compare the analytical predictions with finite element simulations. The model relates the coupler length and width to the frequency splitting and dissipation dilution of the two coupled modes. In the short-coupler limit, $k_cl_c\ll1$, the symmetric-mode coupler undergoes nearly uniform rotation, and its torsional strain energy vanishes asymptotically. The remaining loss contributions arise from polygon-side bending and supporting-tether torsion. The reduced supporting-tether contribution allows the symmetric-mode dissipation dilution to exceed that of an isolated polygon with the same side and supporting-tether dimensions. The antisymmetric mode retains torsional strain in the coupler and has an additional loss contribution. We also derive an expression for $Q\cdot f$ in the short-coupler and short-tether limits, where $Q$ is the mechanical quality factor and $f$ is the resonance frequency. This expression gives the dependence of $Q\cdot f$ on tensile stress, film thickness, and supporting-tether geometry. For a coupler length of $100~μ\mathrm{m}$ and width of $2~μ\mathrm{m}$, finite element calculations give a frequency splitting of $17.7~\mathrm{Hz}$ and a symmetric-mode dilution factor approximately $13\%$ above the analytical isolated-polygon value.

infographic.key_insight: A shared tether tunes frequency splitting and dissipation in coupled square resonators, with short couplers enabling symmetric-mode dissipation dilution above the isolated-polygon value.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupler geometry offers a design lever for controlling mechanical coupling while reducing dissipation in resonator devices.
method: Develop a continuum model of two identical square resonators joined by a shared tether.
Relate coupler dimensions to mode splitting and dissipation dilution; compare predictions with finite element simulations.
Derive short-coupler and short-tether scaling for the quality-factor–frequency product, Q·f.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a 100 μm-long, 2 μm-wide coupler, finite element calculations yield 17.7 Hz frequency splitting and symmetric-mode dilution approximately 13% above the analytical isolated-polygon value.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is simulation-based, and the simplified Q·f expression assumes short couplers and short supporting tethers.
infographic.paper_title: Coupled Soft-Clamped Polygon Resonators with Tunable Mechanical Coupling

title: Allen--Cahn Residual-Constrained Topology Optimization via an Augmented Lagrangian Method
authors: Run Du, Xuan Xiao, Wenming Cheng, Zeqiang Zhang
abstract: This paper presents a residual-constrained topology optimization framework that controls interface transition bandwidth without requiring external density filters. The steady conserved Allen--Cahn (AC) equation is formulated as an equality residual constraint and solved via a mass-weighted Augmented Lagrangian Method (ALM) coupled with the Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA). A closed-form chemical potential projection eliminates the constant residual mode, ensuring algebraic compatibility with external volume targets. Variational sensitivity analysis reveals a symmetric-plus-rank-one Jacobian that yields matrix-free sensitivities without additional adjoint PDE solves, reducing residual sensitivity overhead to only 0.11% of the state elasticity solve time in 3D. Systematic 2D benchmarks confirm that interface bandwidth is governed intrinsically by reaction--diffusion parameters across mesh refinements. While diffuse interfaces incur a continuous compliance elevation (1.4%--12.3%), a volume-preserving 0/1 post-processing audit across 48 benchmark cases demonstrates that this gap stems primarily from intermediate-density penalization: binarized AC-ALM designs achieve equal or superior stiffness in 45 configurations (averaging 1.2% stiffer than SIMP). Simultaneously, single-node hinges and strut fragmentation are substantially suppressed compared to unregularized baselines. Three-dimensional benchmarks further demonstrate practical spatial viability for complex structures.

infographic.key_insight: Constraining the steady conserved Allen–Cahn residual controls topology interface bandwidth intrinsically, without external density filters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach suppresses single-node hinges and strut fragmentation while producing binarized designs with competitive stiffness.
method: Enforce the Allen–Cahn equality residual using a mass-weighted augmented Lagrangian method coupled with MMA.
Project the chemical potential to eliminate the constant residual mode and maintain compatibility with prescribed volume targets.
Exploit a symmetric-plus-rank-one Jacobian for matrix-free residual sensitivities without additional adjoint PDE solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 48 benchmark cases, volume-preserving binarized designs matched or exceeded SIMP stiffness in 45 cases and averaged 1.2% stiffer; reported 3D residual-sensitivity overhead was 0.11% of the elasticity solve time.
infographic.watch_item: Diffuse designs showed 1.4%–12.3% higher compliance, so stiffness gains should be interpreted in the context of the volume-preserving binarization audit.
infographic.paper_title: Allen--Cahn Residual-Constrained Topology Optimization via an Augmented Lagrangian Method

title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures
authors: James Malcolm, Clare McColgan, Emma Mullarkey, Emad Chaparian
abstract: We develop a computational framework to investigate the flow kinematics of viscoplastic materials, described by the Herschel-Bulkley model, in vane-in-cup rheometers. Numerical simulations are performed using augmented Lagrangian finite element and regularised finite volume methods for two- and three-dimensional configurations, respectively, to characterise the hydrodynamics and yielding behaviour over a broad range of effective parameters. Three types of vanes are investigated: conventional 4- and 6-arm bespoke vanes and a 24-arm fractal vane (Owens et al., J. Rheol., vol. 64(3), 2020, 643-662). Our previous two-dimensional study (Chaparian et al., J. Non-Newtonian Fluid Mech., vol. 307, 2022, 104857) demonstrated the superiority of the fractal vane over conventional N-arm designs. The bespoke vanes produce highly non-uniform yielding, leading to significant deviations from the circular Couette analogy, whereas the 24-arm fractal vane generates nearly axisymmetric yield surfaces that effectively "cloak" the vane geometry. Consequently, the resulting flow closely resembles the azimuthal shear in a conventional "bob & cup" rheometer, providing substantially more accurate rheological measurements. Building on these findings, the present study revisits the torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain rate conversions used in vane-in-cup rheometry. In particular, we re-examine the circular Couette analogy that underpins both the physical interpretation of the flow and the extraction of flow curves from raw rheometric data. Based on our extensive two- and three-dimensional simulations, we identify limitations of the existing conversion relations and propose improved closure expressions that enable more accurate determination of material's rheological properties. Furthermore, the three-dimensional flow structures and yielding patterns within the vane-in-cup fixtures are characterised.

infographic.key_insight: Simulations show that a 24-arm fractal vane produces nearly axisymmetric yielding, while improved conversion expressions support more accurate rheological measurements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Better vane designs and torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain-rate conversions can improve characterization of yield-stress materials.
method: Model viscoplastic flow using the Herschel–Bulkley constitutive law.
Use augmented Lagrangian finite elements in 2D and regularised finite volumes in 3D.
Compare 4-arm, 6-arm and 24-arm fractal vanes and revisit circular Couette conversion assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive 2D and 3D simulations across a broad parameter range, but provides no quantitative error reductions or experimental validation details.
infographic.watch_item: This is a numerical rheometry study, not an AI surrogate; conversion accuracy should be checked for the intended geometry and material parameters.
infographic.paper_title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures
